title: dumpcap: Record the processes that packets belong to
description:
Fifth of the series adding capture-time process attribution (design on wireshark-dev: https://lists.wireshark.org/archives/wireshark-dev/202609/msg00002.html; see #17525 and #1184; previous MRs: !26470, !26471, !26479, !26493).

With the file format, the display and the socket lookup in place, this MR makes dumpcap use them: a new `--process-info` option records, for each captured TCP or UDP packet, the processes on the capturing host that sent or received it. It is off by default and costs nothing unless enabled.

**What gets written** (pcapng only): the process IDs in `epb_processid_threadid` options of the packet block, one per process now that the draft allows several (thread ID 0, since the socket tables don't know it), and a Process Information Block describing each process (name, path, command line, parent, user, start time), written once per output file, before the first packet that refers to it, and again in each ring-buffer file. Until the specification assigns the block type, the block is the Wireshark custom block (PEN 32622, entry type 3) that wiretap already reads (!26471), so files open in this Wireshark with the `frame.process.*` fields (!26479) filled in.

**How a packet is attributed**: `wsutil/packet_endpoints.h` (new) extracts the addresses, protocol and ports from the packet for the link-layer types dumpcap commonly sees: Ethernet with VLAN tags, the BSD loopback encapsulations (`LINKTYPE_NULL`/`LOOP`, i.e. macOS `lo0` and Npcap's loopback adapter), Linux cooked capture v1/v2 (the "any" interface) and raw IP; IPv6 extension headers are stepped over and later fragments are rejected since they carry no ports. `capture/capture_process_info.c` (new, dumpcap only) decides which end is on this host, an address of one of the interfaces (listed at start and every 30 s), a loopback address or, for the destination, a broadcast or multicast address, and asks the lookup from !26493 for the processes of that end; both ends of a loopback packet are looked up. What can be identified follows from the lookup: on Windows every process; on Linux the user's own processes, or all of them if dumpcap runs as root or has CAP_SYS_PTRACE (reading another process's `/proc/<pid>/fd` needs that capability unless the process is the user's own and has no capabilities itself). Dumpcap normally clears every capability once the interfaces are open; with `--process-info` it keeps CAP_SYS_PTRACE, and only that, if it has it, since the lookup runs for the whole capture. Without it, the common desktop setup (dumpcap with the two capture capabilities, run by the user) still attributes the user's own processes. On other platforms the option is refused with a message.

**Reading several processes per packet**: since the draft now allows one `epb_processid_threadid` option per process, wiretap registers the option as repeatable and writes every instance (new `wtap_block_get_nth_uint64_option_value()`), and the frame dissector adds a process subtree per instance, so `frame.process.pid` lists them all; the conversation filter and the user name column use the first, which dumpcap writes as the process that has had the socket longest. The multicast case in the earlier discussion works end to end: a datagram sent by one process to a group two other processes have joined is attributed to all three.

**Scale** (measured in the CI container: 3000 addresses on `lo`, 50,000 UDP sockets in 5 processes, 100 network namespaces, 2000 datagrams/s): addresses cost nothing measurable (the local-address set is listed every 30 s, 90 ms for 3000, and looked up by hash); other namespaces' traffic is not attributable and their processes only cost the descriptor scan. Sockets are the cost: a refresh with 50,000 UDP sockets takes about 5 s on Linux, 2.8 s of it the kernel producing `/proc/net/udp`, and refreshing on every miss at most 250 ms apart left dumpcap capturing one packet in 8 s. The lookup now keeps refreshes at least ten times as far apart as the last one took (on top of the 250 ms floor) and warns once when a refresh is slow, so refreshing takes at most a tenth of the time; with that, dumpcap keeps up at ~10 µs of CPU per packet after the first refresh under the same load. The remaining costs, the first refresh and late attribution of sockets created between refreshes, call for netlink `sock_diag` instead of the text tables (5× faster for the same dump) and refreshing in a thread; both are Linux-only follow-ups.

**Plumbing**: `--process-info` is a common capture option (`ui/capture_opts.c`), so TShark and Wireshark accept it and pass it to dumpcap; dumpcap refuses it with pcap output. `writecap` gains `pcapng_write_process_information_block()` and process IDs on `pcapng_write_enhanced_packet_block()`. Man pages for dumpcap, tshark and wireshark, and the release notes, are updated. There is no Qt preference yet; that is the last MR of the series.

**Tests**: `test_wsutil` gains packet-parser tests for each link-layer type, VLAN tags, IPv6 extension headers, fragments, non-TCP/UDP packets and truncation. `suite_capture.py` gains `TestCaptureProcessInfo`, which captures the test suite's own UDP traffic on loopback with `--process-info`, with dumpcap and with TShark, and checks with tshark that every packet is attributed to the test process by PID, with its name and path, so both the writer and the reader are exercised end to end; a third test starts two receiver processes on one UDP port and checks that datagrams to it are attributed to the sender and both receivers. The tests skip where the option is not supported. `suite_dissection.py` and `suite_fileformats.py` gain tests on a generated capture with several processes per packet, including that editcap preserves them.

**Not in this MR**: the macOS backend, and the "exact" packet-level modes (eBPF/ETW/PKTAP).

Built and tested on Windows (MSVC; capture tests on the Npcap loopback adapter), Linux (the CI container: GCC, Clang + code checks, ASAN; capture tests on `lo` both as an unprivileged user with dumpcap carrying the capture capabilities and as root, and a manual check that a multicast datagram sent from one process to two subscribed receiver processes is attributed to all three) and macOS (Apple clang; option refused as unsupported, tests skip).

I measured it, and it found a real problem, now fixed in the amended commit. Setup in the CI container: 3000 addresses on `lo`, 50,000 UDP sockets in 5 processes, 100 network namespaces each with a process holding a socket, 2000 datagrams/s to alternating addresses.

Thousands of addresses are cheap: they only feed the set that decides which end of a packet is local, listed with `pcap_findalldevs()` every 30 s (90 ms for 3000 addresses) and looked up by hash per packet. Namespaces are invisible rather than expensive: dumpcap sees the socket tables of its own network namespace, so traffic of other namespaces captured on a bridge or veth simply gets no attribution; their processes still get their `/proc/<pid>/fd` scanned, at about 16 µs per descriptor.

The problem was sockets. A refresh of the snapshot reads `/proc/net/{tcp,udp}{,6}` and scans every process's descriptors; with 50,000 UDP sockets that is 2.8 s for the kernel to produce `/proc/net/udp` plus 0.8 s for the scan, about 5 s in all, and the first version refreshed on every miss at most 250 ms apart, so under that load dumpcap refreshed back to back, captured one packet in 8 s and dropped the rest. The fix in wsutil: a miss now triggers a refresh only if at least ten times the duration of the last refresh has passed (with the 250 ms floor), so refreshing never takes more than a tenth of the time, and a warning says so once when a refresh takes over half a second. Same setup afterwards: dumpcap keeps up at \~10 µs of CPU per packet after the first refresh, every captured packet attributed; the cost that remains is that first refresh, during which the capture buffer can overflow on a host like that, and that sockets created between refreshes are attributed late.

Two follow-ups would take that further, both Linux-only and separable: reading the sockets through netlink `sock_diag` instead of the text tables (`ss` dumps the same 50,000 sockets in 0.5 s, the raw dump is faster still), and running refreshes in a thread so the capture loop never waits; per-namespace tables (`/proc/<pid>/net`) would make container traffic attributable. For a traffic simulator that also churns connections faster than the refresh interval, the honest answer is the packet-level "exact" mode (eBPF/ETW), which is on the list after this series. I'd rather land the bounded version now and do those as their own MRs, unless you'd like the netlink reader in this one.
There's a few things I'd like to fix in this MR. I'll get back on it 18/09/2026 when my Fable resets.

How do these changes handle process ID wraparound?

If a system were to create one process per millisecond, it would take about 25 days for an always-positive 32-bit signed `pid_t`, with a maximum value of 2^31-1, to wrap around.

Process IDs are reused within a capture already on ordinary hosts (Linux's default pid_max of 32768 wraps in under a minute on a busy build server), so the design treats the PID as a reusable key and the start time as the disambiguator, which is what the draft's pib_starttime is for. In wsutil the lookup keeps one record per process with its start time (boot time plus start tick on Linux, creation time on Windows); a refresh that finds a PID with a different start time creates a new record. Dumpcap keys "already described in this file" by those records, so a reused PID gets a new Process Information Block, written before its first packet. Wiretap resolves a packet's PID to the latest block for it whose start time is at or before the packet's timestamp, falling back to the first if all of them start later. Once epb_pib_index is assigned, dumpcap will write it as well, which makes the reference exact.

Limits: two incarnations within one Linux clock tick (10 ms) can't be told apart by start time; a process reusing both the PID and the socket tuple of its predecessor within one refresh interval is attributed to the predecessor until the next refresh, which is inherent to polling and is what the packet-level exact modes will fix; and a writer that records no start times gets no disambiguation. For the last one, and for clock skew, I plan a wiretap follow-up that breaks ties by file order, since every writer so far emits a block before the first packet that uses it.

The wiretap follow-up I mentioned is !26550: a packet is now matched only against the process information blocks that precede it in the file, since every writer so far describes a process before the first packet it attributes to it, and among those the start times decide as before; when none has a usable start time, or all of them are later than the packet, the last block before it wins instead of the first. That covers writers without start times and clock skew, and the reuse case in the generated test captures reads the way one would expect.

+/** @file

+ * Attribute captured packets to the processes on this host that sent or
+ * received them, by looking their sockets up while capturing.
+ *
+ * Wireshark - Network traffic analyzer

+
+#ifndef __CAPTURE_PROCESS_INFO_H__
+#define __CAPTURE_PROCESS_INFO_H__
+
+#include <wireshark.h>
+#include <wsutil/process_lookup.h>
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+extern "C" {
+#endif /* __cplusplus */
+
+typedef struct capture_process_info capture_process_info_t;
+
+/**
+ * A function that lists the capture interfaces, with their addresses, as
+ * capture_options.get_iface_list does.
+ */
+typedef GList *(*capture_process_info_iface_list_func)(int *err, char **err_str);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Set up to attribute packets to processes.
+ *
+ * @param get_iface_list Lists this host's interfaces; their addresses say
+ * which end of a packet is on this host.
+ * @param err_msg Set to a g_malloc()ed message if this fails.
+ * @return The context, or NULL if process information is not available.
+ */
+extern capture_process_info_t *
+capture_process_info_new(capture_process_info_iface_list_func get_iface_list,
+                         char **err_msg);
+
+extern void
+capture_process_info_free(capture_process_info_t *cpi);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Whether packets with a link-layer header type can be attributed.
+ *
+ * @param linktype The LINKTYPE_ value of the interface.
+ */
+extern bool
+capture_process_info_linktype_supported(int linktype);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Find the processes that sent or received a packet.
+ *
+ * They are the processes that have a socket matching the end of the packet
+ * that is on this host: one of its addresses or, for the destination, a
+ * broadcast or multicast address. Both ends of a loopback packet are.
+ *
+ * @param cpi The context.
+ * @param linktype The LINKTYPE_ value of the packet.
+ * @param data The packet data.
+ * @param len The number of bytes captured.
+ * @param processes What is known about each process is appended, as const
+ * ws_process_info_t pointers valid until the context is freed.
+ * @return The number of processes appended.
+ */
+extern unsigned
+capture_process_info_lookup(capture_process_info_t *cpi, int linktype,
+                            const uint8_t *data, size_t len,
+                            GPtrArray *processes);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Forget which processes the output file already describes.
+ *
+ * Call when starting a new output file.
+ */
+extern void
+capture_process_info_new_file(capture_process_info_t *cpi);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Whether a process still has to be described in the output file.
+ *
+ * @return true the first time it is called for a process since the file
+ * was started; the process then counts as described.
+ */
+extern bool
+capture_process_info_needs_description(capture_process_info_t *cpi,
+                                       const ws_process_info_t *process);
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+}
+#endif /* __cplusplus */
+
+#endif /* __CAPTURE_PROCESS_INFO_H__ */

 The following features are either new or have been significantly updated since version 4.6.0:
 
+* Dumpcap, TShark and Wireshark can record which processes on the capturing host sent or received each packet, with the new `--process-info` capture option: the process IDs go in the pcapng epb_processid_threadid packet option and the processes (name, path, command line, parent, user, start time) are described in process information blocks, shown as the `frame.process` fields. +def gen_several_processes() -> None:
+    """process_info_several.pcapng: packets that belong to several processes,
+    one epb_processid_threadid option each, e.g. a multicast datagram and
+    its sender and receivers."""
+    base_ts = 1_757_600_000_000_000
+
+    def pib(pid: int, name: bytes) -> bytes:
+        return wireshark_cb("<", wireshark_cb_custom_data(WIRESHARK_CB_ENTRY_PROCESS_INFORMATION,
+                                                          pib_entry(pid, [(OPT_PIB_NAME, name)])))
+
+    def packet(seq: int, pids) -> bytes:
+        return epb("<", base_ts + seq, udp_packet(seq),
+                   [(OPT_EPB_PROCESSID_THREADID, struct.pack("<II", pid, 0)) for pid in pids])
+
+    out = shb("<") + idb("<")
+    out += pib(10, b"sender") + pib(20, b"receiver") + pib(30, b"other")
+    out += packet(1, [10, 20, 30])
+    out += packet(2, [20])
+    write("process_info_several.pcapng", out)
+

commits_data.title: dumpcap: Record the processes that packets belong to
commits_data.message:
dumpcap: Record the processes that packets belong to

Add --process-info, which makes dumpcap look each captured TCP or UDP
packet up in the operating system's socket tables and record, in the
pcapng file, the processes on the capturing host that sent or received
it: their IDs in epb_processid_threadid options of the packet block, and
a description of each process (name, executable path, command line,
parent, user, start time) in a process information block, written once
per output file before the first packet that refers to it. Until the
pcapng specification assigns a block type to the process information
block, it is written as a Wireshark custom block, PEN 32622 entry type 3,
which wiretap already reads.

A packet's end on this host is the one whose address is an address of
one of the host's interfaces, a loopback address or, for the destination,
a broadcast or multicast address; both ends of a loopback packet are.
The processes are the ones wsutil's process lookup finds for that end,
so what can be identified depends on the platform and privileges, as
documented in the man pages. On Linux, seeing the sockets of processes
other than the user's own takes CAP_SYS_PTRACE, so with --process-info
dumpcap keeps that capability, and only that, if it has it, when it
drops the others after opening the interfaces.

Add wsutil/packet_endpoints.h, which finds the addresses, protocol and
ports of a packet captured with Ethernet (with VLAN tags), the BSD
loopback encapsulations, Linux cooked capture v1 or v2, or raw IP, with
IPv6 extension headers stepped over and later fragments rejected, and
writecap functions to write the process information block and the
epb_processid_threadid options.

TShark and Wireshark accept the option too and pass it on to dumpcap.

The pcapng draft now allows several epb_processid_threadid options in
a packet block, one per process that could have sent or received the
packet, so wiretap accepts and writes several, with a new
wtap_block_get_nth_uint64_option_value(), and the frame dissector
shows every process of a packet, e.g. the sender and the receivers of
a multicast datagram on the capturing host.

On a host with very many sockets, reading the socket tables is slow
(about 5 s with 50,000 UDP sockets on Linux, most of it the kernel
producing /proc/net/udp), and refreshing them on every miss, 250 ms
apart, left dumpcap no time to capture. wsutil's lookup now keeps
refreshes at least ten times as far apart as the last one took, so
that they never take more than a tenth of the time, and warns once
when a refresh is slow.

Add unit tests for the packet parser, capture tests that record the
test process's own traffic with dumpcap and with TShark, and with two
receiver processes, and a generated capture with several processes per
packet.

Related to #1184 and #17525.
